## #1 2026 US midterm elections

_Trending on bluesky, mastodon, news, wikipedia (57 signals, 24 outlets)_

### The main story

Most groups describe the 2026 US midterms as a sweeping Democratic win, often called a 'blue wave' or 'sweep'. Democrats flipped dozens of House seats and made gains in state legislatures, while some Senate races, such as Mississippi and Alaska, were still being counted. Coverage turns to what Democrats will do with their new power and how President Trump will respond.

### Points of disagreement

- WION (Indian media) says Democrats are poised for their biggest House majority since 1991, while NDTV (Indian media, centrist) says since 2008.
- The Washington Post (US media, left-leaning) says Democrats are favored to win a 'slim' House majority, while WION (Indian media) says they are closing in on about 260 seats, a historic majority.

### Analysis details
**Divide verdict: strong**
(labeller agreement kappa 0.58; 51/160 items took a clear framing)

| Framing | Meaning | Share of framed items |
|---|---|---|
| Live results and vote tracking | Posts present the midterms as a running tally of races, maps and charts, reporting who won or leads without much interpretation. | 33% |
| Democratic mandate and governing agenda | Posts treat the Democratic win of Congress and state legislatures as a mandate and look at what the party will do with power, such as tariff reversal, Supreme Court reform, election law changes, AI limits and leadership choices. | 10% |
| Republican and Trump fallout | Posts focus on the Republican defeat as a rebuke of Trump and a source of turmoil, covering aides doubting his focus, White House staff changes, 2028 worries and the Iran war. | 29% |
| Markets, business and economy | Posts view the results through their financial effects, including falling stocks, AI-sector jitters, business implications and policy forecasts. | 12% |
| Voter blocs and long-term political shifts | Posts interpret the results as evidence of wider trends, such as women voters, progressive versus moderate Democrats, populism, historical comparisons and the 2028 outlook. | 16% |

Coverage of the 2026 US midterms splits across five framings, though only 51 of 160 items (32%) carried one. The divide is rated strong (kappa 0.58).

The largest framing, live results and vote tracking (33%), presents tallies, maps and charts with little interpretation. In the headline evidence it appears from Reuters, NBC News, Bloomberg, the Financial Times and CBS News. Republican and Trump fallout (29%) frames the result as a rebuke and a source of turmoil. It appears in headlines from PBS, AP, MS NOW, CNN and The Telegraph, and in posts from mastodon:killbait. Voter blocs and long-term shifts (16%) shows up at The Washington Post, The Conversation, CNN and SBS. Markets and business (12%) appears at the Financial Times, Bloomberg, CNBC and The Japan Times' Mastodon account. Democratic mandate and governing agenda (10%) is the smallest, with CBS News, SBS and mastodon:DrALJONES as examples.

Several outlets span more than one framing. Bloomberg, CNN and the FT each appear in two.

Limits: every outlet and account is still marked "building," with only 1 to 4 outlet items and 1 to 13 account items each. Outlet leanings are inferred from headlines and snippets, and the data supplies no lean labels. Sample sizes are small.

## #2 Data center backlash

_Trending on mastodon, news (11 signals, 8 outlets)_

### The main story

Opposition to data centers has grown into a visible political and protest movement. US midterm results are widely described as a voter rebuke tied to data center and AI expansion, with tech firms such as OpenAI and Meta responding. Protests have also spread to Europe, including an incident in which activists entered a Microsoft data center site in Amsterdam.

### How each side differs

**Hacker News comments** (58 items; 28304283409234, Animats, AnthonyMouse, DrewADesign, Grombobulous, MantisShrimp90, PorciiVorbesc, ProfessorLayton)  
Commenters debate causes rather than report events. They offer explanations such as anger over gas and grocery prices, hostility to AI itself rather than to data centers, and tech industry 'arrogant, high-handed' siting with NDAs and 'suborned' local governments. Some suggest pitching renewables on cost predictability, and others argue the industry did foresee the backlash, citing secrecy and space data centers.

- Hacker News comments, US media (centrist): commenters attribute the backlash to prices or to AI generally, while Big Tech, as reported by Ars Technica, says voters' anger is 'anti-Trump' rather than 'anti-tech'.

_12 items came from outlets whose origin is unknown and are not attributed to any side._

### Analysis details
**Divide verdict: unreliable**
(labeller agreement kappa 0.22; 24/140 items took a clear framing)

| Framing | Meaning | Share of framed items |
|---|---|---|
| Midterms as voter verdict | Frames data center opposition as a decisive electoral force, citing ousted incumbents, flipped states and ballot results as a message from voters. | 4% |
| Industry response and damage control | Covers how tech companies and suppliers react to the backlash through pledges, rebranding, retrofitting ideas, warnings about slower expansion, and arguments that the anger is political rather than anti-tech. | 4% |
| Backlash as business and market risk | Treats the backlash as a financial and strategic matter, examining effects on energy stocks, IPOs, the trillion-dollar buildout, and which large or small firms gain or lose. | 8% |
| European street protest and direct action | Reports on physical demonstrations and site break-ins across Europe, presenting the opposition as a spreading, coordinated protest movement. | 54% |
| Regulation, politicians and civil liberties | Focuses on political targets and policy consequences, including protests at a senator's home, expected tougher rules, and arguments about civil rights and accountability of big tech deals. | 29% |

Coverage of the data center backlash splits into five framings, though only 24 of 140 items (17%) were framed, and agreement between coders was low (kappa 0.22, rated unreliable). The divide is therefore hard to measure.

The largest framing, at 54% of framed items (13 of 24), is European street protest and direct action. It presents the opposition as a spreading protest movement. Seattle Times, Los Angeles Times, Gadget Review, Briefs Finance, Times of India and tech-insider.org headlines fit it, mostly the Amsterdam Microsoft site entry.

Regulation, politicians and civil liberties follows at 29% (7 items). The ACLU piece and several Hacker News commenters (Grombobulous, drweevil, reasonableklout, dam_jackalopes, pj_mukh) fit it, raising regulation, NDAs and accountability.

Smaller framings:
- Business and market risk (2 items): Financial Times and Business Insider.
- Industry damage control (1 item): BankInfoSecurity, on OpenAI easing the backlash.
- Midterms as voter verdict (1 item): one Hacker News comment from ProfessorLayton.

No outlet or account has a stable lean label; all are still marked "building," with 1 to 2 items each against thresholds of 10 and 15. Outlets are judged only from headlines and snippets, and the samples are very small, so these attributions are tentative.

## #3 College football weekend

_Trending on bluesky, google_trends, news (16 signals, 3 outlets)_

### The main story

The items are a scattered mix about college football and college sports rather than one single event. ### Analysis details
**Divide verdict: strong**
(labeller agreement kappa 0.6; 43/160 items took a clear framing)

| Framing | Meaning | Share of framed items |
|---|---|---|
| Playoff race and rankings implications | Pieces treat each result mainly as a shift in the CFP and AP rankings, asking who is in, out or on the brink after upsets and the first committee release. | 37% |
| Practical viewing guides and schedules | Posts serve fans with live updates, schedules, TV information, GameDay locations and lists of the best games to watch. | 35% |
| Upset alerts and weekend drama | Previews and recaps build tension around ranked teams at risk, teams with no room for error, and top-ranked sides falling. | 14% |
| Skepticism toward the ranking process | Some items question the legitimacy of the committee and rankings, calling the show pointless, taking digs at the SEC and offering alternative rankings of how they should look. | 12% |
| Cost and fan-experience burden | An item focuses on the financial side of attending big games, such as steep hotel prices and ticket costs. | 2% |

College football weekend coverage splits into five framings, and the divide is rated strong (kappa 0.6). Only 43 of 160 items (27%) carried a framing, so the picture rests on a minority of the sample.

The two largest framings are close in size. "Playoff race and rankings implications" (37%) treats results as shifts in the CFP and AP rankings. "Practical viewing guides and schedules" (35%) serves fans with schedules, TV details and GameDay locations. Smaller are "Upset alerts and weekend drama" (14%), "Skepticism toward the ranking process" (12%) and "Cost and fan-experience burden" (2%, one item).

Outlet examples, with no political or ideological labels in the data:
- Playoff implications: Yahoo, On3, FanSided.
- Viewing guides: NCAA.com, ESPN, Sportsnaut, Yahoo Sports.
- Upset drama: The Guardian, Sports Illustrated, CBS Sports.
- Skepticism: SportsGrid.
- Cost: Fox News.

Among accounts, deadline and variety_feed lean toward viewing guides, while rydunleavy appears under both drama and skepticism.

Limits: every outlet and account is still marked "building," with about one to three items each. Placements come from headlines and snippets, so they are tentative.

## #4 Stephen Miller named chief of staff

_Trending on news, wikipedia (9 signals, 6 outlets)_

### The main story

President Trump announced that Stephen Miller, the White House deputy chief of staff and the architect of his immigration crackdown, will replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff. Outlets generally tie the move to Republican losses in the midterm elections and describe Miller as a hardliner.

### Analysis details
**Divide verdict: unreliable**
(labeller agreement kappa 0.42; 33/160 items took a clear framing)

| Framing | Meaning | Share of framed items |
|---|---|---|
| Neutral personnel announcement | Straight news reports state that Trump named Stephen Miller chief of staff to replace Susie Wiles, with little added interpretation. | 12% |
| Reaction to midterm losses | Posts tie the staffing change to Republican midterm defeats, presenting it as Trump's first major move after the election, sometimes with language like 'fires', 'blowout' or 'wipeout'. | 39% |
| Alarm about Miller's influence | Coverage quotes a former Trump aide calling the prospect of Miller replacing Wiles 'terrifying', framing the change as a source of concern. | 15% |
| Promotion and profile of Miller | Pieces present the move as a promotion or explain who Miller is, including biographical angles such as his Duke background. | 33% |

Coverage of Stephen Miller replacing Susie Wiles as chief of staff splits into four framings, though only 33 of 160 items (21%) carried a framing. Reaction to midterm losses is the largest (39%). It links the change to Republican defeats, sometimes with words like "fires," "blowout" or "rout." Promotion and profile of Miller follows (33%), covering his background and the hard-line agenda. Alarm about Miller's influence (15%) quotes a former aide calling the prospect "terrifying." The neutral announcement framing is smallest (12%), though several outlets' headlines read this way.

The divide looks modest and unstable: kappa is 0.42, which the data rates "unreliable."

No outlet or account carries a political-lean label, so none can be placed on a side. By headline, WSJ, NPR, CNBC, Axios, DW, The Economist and Politico mostly used neutral announcement wording. The New York Post, The Independent, The Times of Israel, NDTV and The Times of India used midterm-loss language. The New York Times and The Telegraph leaned toward profile. Mastodon accounts split between midterm-loss and alarm posts.

Limits: outlets are judged from headlines and snippets, and each has only 2–3 items, below the thresholds for a reliable read.

## #5 Krakow shooting

_Trending on bluesky, news (17 signals, 10 outlets)_

### The main story

A gunman opened fire in Krakow's Main Market Square in Poland on a busy Saturday, and most outlets report at least six people killed and about 15 injured. Police shot and detained the suspect, and bodies were reportedly found at his home. Officials described the suspect as holding far-right or ultranationalist views.

### Points of disagreement

- Death toll: Indian media (ANI, The Hindu), NDTV Profit and Asharq Al-Awsat (UK media) say 5 killed, while most other groups say 6; India Today (Indian media) and NBC 7 San Diego (US media) say 9 killed.
- Injured count: The Hindu says 12 and ANI says 'dozens', while most outlets say 15 and PBS, Moneycontrol and one other report 16.
- Bodies at the suspect's home: Moneycontrol, USA Today, CBS and The Statesman say 3 found there. CBS frames them as additional dead beyond the six, and some other outlets treat the toll as six total.

_1 items came from outlets whose origin is unknown and are not attributed to any side._

### Analysis details
**Divide verdict: strong**
(labeller agreement kappa 0.87; 76/93 items took a clear framing)

| Framing | Meaning | Share of framed items |
|---|---|---|
| Breaking news incident reporting | Headlines focus on the unfolding event, giving casualty counts, location in the market square, and police statements, with figures that shift between five, six and nine dead. | 62% |
| Far-right ideology as motive | Articles foreground officials' statements that the gunman was fascinated by far-right or ultranationalist ideas, treating ideology as the key explanatory detail. | 18% |
| Terror attack and official response | Posts quote police and government figures describing the shooting as an act of terror and report on the investigation, including bodies found at the suspect's home. | 9% |
| National mourning and shock | Coverage emphasizes grief, communal and church reaction, and a country in shock over an attack in a historic public space. | 5% |
| Eyewitness footage and personal stories | Items highlight video of gunshots and people taking cover, plus individual survivor accounts, to convey the experience on the ground. | 5% |

Coverage of the Krakow shooting is strongly divided by framing (kappa 0.87), with 76 of 93 items (82%) assigned a framing. Breaking-news incident reporting dominates at 62% (47 items). Headlines in this frame give casualty counts, the market-square location and police statements, and the death toll varies between five, six and nine.

Smaller framings follow:
- Far-right ideology as motive (18%, 14 items) foregrounds officials' statements that the gunman held far-right or ultranationalist views.
- Terror attack and official response (9%, 7 items) quotes police and government describing an act of terror and covers the investigation, including bodies found at the suspect's home.
- National mourning and shock (5%, 4 items) stresses grief and communal reaction.
- Eyewitness footage and personal stories (5%, 4 items) centers on video and survivor accounts.

No outlet or account carries a political-lean label. Each has only one sampled item, so the data does not show consistent leanings. Examples: CBS, BBC, Guardian, Bloomberg, ABC, PBS, NDTV, Politico, Jerusalem Post and Asharq Al-Awsat appear under incident reporting; AP under ideology; Yahoo and Reuters under mourning and shock; CNN and Euronews under footage.

Limits: outlets are judged from headlines and snippets only, and the samples are small, so these patterns are tentative.

## #6 ICE enforcement controversies

_Trending on bluesky, news (7 signals, 4 outlets)_

### The main story

Items across groups describe a run of controversies over ICE enforcement, including local agreements and policies on cooperating with ICE (Houston, Nassau County, Maricopa County, 287(g)), the detention and release of a Wisconsin state trooper, and the leadership of ICE and Stephen Miller's role. Several outlets also tie the topic to the midterm elections and to public criticism of ICE tactics.

**Mastodon posts** (78 items; CharlieMcHenry@connectop.us, CubitOom@social.linux.pizza, FinchHaven@hachyderm.io, GetMisch@masto.nyc, JaZone@universeodon.com, KimPerales@toad.social, MaKaNaS@tardigram.com, MikeDunnAuthor@kolektiva.social)

| Explainer and insider perspective | Offers informational or expert-led background on what ICE is, what powers agents have and why enforcement has become aggressive, often through former officials or legal analysts. | 19% |

**Briefing: ICE enforcement controversies**

Across 160 items, only 21 (13%) carried a distinct framing, and the divide is rated weak (kappa 0.69). Most coverage did not clearly adopt any frame.

Five framings appear. The most common is local-federal cooperation disputes (33%), covering 287(g) agreements and Houston's police policy. Next is waste and harm critique (29%), which cites costs and individual cases. Explainer and insider perspective follows (19%), then accountability and legal limits (10%) and Trump policy and personnel (10%).

The data gives no political-lean labels, only framing evidence from single items. The Guardian and CNN headlines fit the waste and harm frame. BBC, CBC, Politico and the Brennan Center fit the explainer frame. The New York Times, Fox News and the ACLU fit the cooperation frame, and Brookings fits accountability. The Council on Foreign Relations fits the Trump-policy frame. Several Mastodon accounts match harm or Trump-policy framings, while one account is mostly neutral across 21 items.

Limits: outlets are judged from headlines and snippets, each outlet has one item, and every label is still marked as building. Sample sizes are small, so these patterns are tentative.

### Analysis details
**Divide verdict: strong**
(labeller agreement kappa 0.75; 81/160 items took a clear framing)

| Framing | Meaning | Share of framed items |
|---|---|---|
| Straight announcement of the offer | Reports Trump's Truth Social post as a neutral news event, stating that he offered or asked White to become White House press secretary. | 51% |
| White's response and next steps | Follows how White reacted, including his plan to meet Trump, his trip to DC, and conflicting reports that he declined or appeared to accept. | 27% |
| Combative political context | Ties the offer to Trump's language about defending against the 'lunatic left' and to his calls for criminal probes of Democrats, placing the job in a partisan fight. | 9% |
| Personality and spectacle angle | Presents the offer through White's persona and Trump's dramatic wording, with phrases like 'please take the job', 'publicly begs', and 'violent fighter and warrior', or through explainers on who White is. | 14% |

Coverage of Trump's reported offer to Dana White of the White House press secretary job splits into four framings, with a strong divide (kappa 0.75). Of 160 items, 81 (51%) were framed.

**Framings:** The largest, at 41 items (51% of framed), is a straight announcement that Trump offered or asked White to take the role. The second, at 22 (27%), follows White's response: his plan to meet Trump, and conflicting reports that he declined or appeared to accept. A personality and spectacle angle accounts for 11 (14%), using phrases like 'please take the job'. The smallest, at 7 (9%), places the offer in a combative partisan context, citing the 'lunatic left'.

**Outlet leanings:** The data gives no political labels, only framings from single headlines. CBS News, The Washington Post, The Guardian, Bloomberg, PBS, Reuters, CNBC, NewsNation, The Telegraph and the Financial Times lean toward the straight announcement. CNN, Yahoo and The New York Times lean toward White's response. BBC and The Jerusalem Post lean toward spectacle.

**Accounts:** Most Mastodon accounts sampled post straight announcements. KimPerales and DemocracyMattersALot lean toward the combative framing, while deadline and kurtsh lean toward spectacle. lapatilla.com leans toward White's response.

**Limits:** Outlets and accounts are judged from one headline or snippet each, and all are marked as still building. Samples are small, so these placements are tentative.

## #8 Iran war

_Trending on news (19 signals, 13 outlets)_

### The main story

Reports describe a US naval blockade of Iran being widened to include a task force aimed at disrupting Iranian land transport routes. Tankers caught fire in or near the Strait of Hormuz, with Iranian-linked accounts citing naval mines. Coverage also centres on whether Trump will resume full-scale fighting after the Democratic midterm sweep, and on US offers of about $20 million for information on Iran's nuclear programme.
Sources: [CBS News](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiigFBVV95cUxPTGRhLVU1VTVqNWp4WUduNU5uT1pwOEUwYnV1RmlnODdlUzduZDdsLTQzMkZLeVdiYlhBT09pMTI5RGN1a0NYVTl4Y3NDcmV2Q3BKZHJBZ1hEMTZsVXAwZkRyMGxZNDRYVXoyVV9qUXFoaDZrcHNmdXZwaEhMSE9raDJoSlM3a0Z4UVE?oc=5), [The Washington Post](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiyAFBVV95cUxNTHJ4Z08xMkRQRml0cEZYUFhnRmJ2X294S2tERkkwNTN4MjdVVmxqcE5UOWJEZlI1eFlSSXo0RFI3Wnp2bjJlc1JiV2xNX0ljMGUxN1RRU29OV2M3VVp2OWlubzdOSlBOajE2N0h6bEVXbm9QY1lkaXNXbEV1NUdSSXEyQkFZb2VvUzVJNzYtS3pKUFVaUG1Jd0JJN3liMVFWOXJ2a2U0ZlVHY04wdVZFVk1yVzZCNm9MLW81NkNzNGE3czVXWm9HMg?oc=5), [The Hindu](https://news.google.?oc=5), [The Indian Express](https://news.google.?oc=5)

### How each side differs

**Mastodon posts** (80 items; Allkinds, BrentD@techhub.social, DrALJONES, KimPerales@toad.social, LThinkTank, PDFlynn@universeodon.com, RonSupportsYou, ScottLucas@journa.host)  
Posts mix OSINT-style alerts with partisan commentary. One says the IRGC claimed it attacked two tankers, one of them near the UAE coast, quoting an Iranian navy statement in Persian. Another says the vessel was running without identification or navigation systems. Others add a claimed Russian missile resupply of Iran, an unverified report of a thwarted Israeli operation before its 27 Oct election, and the line that oil traders see the war as over. One tracker counts 'Day 252' of the 'US War on Iran', and another post criticises Europe's stance.
Translated from: French
Sources: [faab64@todon.eu](https://todon.eu/@faab64/117577421949370330), [analytics@social.vir.group](https://social.vir.group/@analytics/117563404632092102), [KimPerales@toad.social](https://toad.social/@KimPerales/117577682858850242)

**Indian media** (10 items; BusinessLine, India Today, Indiatimes, Investing.com India, Mid-Day, Moneycontrol.com, News18, Outlook India)  
Coverage stresses effects on India and the markets. Indiatimes reports Iran exempting Indian ships from Hormuz curbs, seen as a positive for the chemicals and pharma sectors, and BusinessLine cites an IEA warning of tight winter gas supply. Headlines also carry Trump's claim that the US is 'not at war' with Iran and that 'nobody' was hurt or killed in five months. A Riyadh early-warning alert and Qatar's mediation role also appear.
Sources: [Indiatimes](https://news.google.?oc=5), [BusinessLine](https://news.google.?oc=5), [News18](https://news.google.?oc=5)

**US media (centrist)** (9 items; Al-Monitor, Axios, Bloomberg.com, CBS News, CNBC, Houston Chronicle, Institute for the Study of War, Scripps News)  
These outlets frame events as US policy and political fallout. They cite CNBC's view that escalation risk stays high despite the midterms, Trump's 'finish the job' stance, and a 'frank' Trump–Netanyahu call. Al-Monitor reports Iran turning to Putin, and Scripps contrasts the bounty with Trump's claims of having 'obliterated' the programme. The ISW daily update and a Houston Chronicle piece on oil company profits add military and economic detail.

### Points of disagreement

- Cause of the tanker fires: Mastodon posts quote the IRGC navy as saying it attacked two 'violating' tankers, while The Hindu, Al Arabiya and an OSINT post say the vessels hit mines.
- Number of tankers: The Hindu and Mastodon's IRGC post report two tankers on fire, while Al Arabiya, Sout Al Emarat and the OSINT post describe a single tanker east of Hormuz.
- Military activity: KOMO and the New York Post report Trump confirming new US strikes near Hormuz, and NDTV reports explosions on Qeshm. A Mastodon war tracker headline says oil prices fell as the 'threat of strikes recedes', and News18 quotes Trump saying the US is not at war and nobody was hurt or killed in five months.

_4 items came from outlets whose origin is unknown and are not attributed to any side._

### Analysis details
**Divide verdict: strong**
(labeller agreement kappa 0.59; 77/160 items took a clear framing)

| Framing | Meaning | Share of framed items |
|---|---|---|
| Live military operations and blockade | Reports tactical developments such as strikes, the naval blockade, the new land-route task force, vessels fired upon and mines, mostly in a factual, event-by-event style. | 57% |
| Diplomacy and de-escalation tracks | Presents talks, the Qatari plan for nuclear inspections, reopening the Strait of Hormuz, and international calls for restraint as a possible path out of the conflict. | 8% |
| Domestic politics and midterm fallout | Treats the war through U.S. electoral and intra-party dynamics, including the midterm results, GOP criticism, clashing advisers, and accountability for the president and Hegseth. | 21% |
| Official US triumph and resolve | Relays administration messaging that portrays the war as courageous and historic, stresses finishing the job, and cites progress and blockade effectiveness. | 4% |
| Skeptical assessments of war outcomes | Questions official claims by pointing to the nuclear-information bounty, reported US-Israeli failures, oil company profits, and escalation risk. | 10% |

Coverage of the Iran war divides strongly (kappa 0.59). Of 160 items, 77 (48%) carried an identifiable framing. The largest, "Live military operations and blockade" (57%), reports strikes, the blockade, the land-route task force and mines in a mostly factual, event-by-event style. "Domestic politics and midterm fallout" follows (21%), covering GOP criticism, adviser clashes and accountability for the president and Hegseth. "Skeptical assessments of war outcomes" (10%) questions official claims, citing oil profits and reported US-Israeli failures. "Diplomacy and de-escalation tracks" (8%) centers on the Qatari plan to reopen Hormuz. "Official US triumph and resolve" is smallest (4%).

Outlet labels come only from single headlines. CBS, The Washington Post, NDTV, Reuters and Euronews fit the operations framing. The Guardian fits diplomacy. Yahoo fits domestic politics. Houston Chronicle, The Jerusalem Post and The Telegraph fit the skeptical framing. Among accounts, analytics, ScottLucas and several others post operational updates. DrALJONES, alternet and RonSupportsYou lean toward domestic politics. dailytimes.com.pk and KimPerales span two framings each.

Limits: outlets are judged from headlines and snippets, each has only one item, and account samples are small (1-4 items). The data does not support firm outlet-level conclusions.
